# Computation of $\pi_1(\mathbb{RP}^n)$ and $\pi_1(\mathrm{Kl}^2)$

## Part I. $\pi_1(\mathbb{RP}^n)$

### Setup: the covering $p:S^n \to \mathbb{RP}^n$

Real projective space $\mathbb{RP}^n$ is the quotient of $S^n \subset \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ by the equivalence relation $x \sim -x$. The quotient map
$$p:S^n \to \mathbb{RP}^n,\qquad p(x)=[x]=\{x,-x\}$$
is a 2-sheeted covering map. Indeed, for any $[x]\in\mathbb{RP}^n$, a small evenly-covered neighborhood $U$ is the image under $p$ of a small ball $B\subset S^n$ around $x$ chosen so that $B\cap(-B)=\varnothing$; then $p^{-1}(U)=B\sqcup(-B)$, with $p|_B$ and $p|_{-B}$ homeomorphisms onto $U$.

### Case $n=0$

$S^0=\{-1,+1\}$ and $\mathbb{RP}^0$ is a single point. Hence
$$\pi_1(\mathbb{RP}^0)=\{1\}.$$

### Case $n=1$

$S^1\to\mathbb{RP}^1$ identifies antipodal points. The map $\theta\mapsto e^{i\theta}$ gives a homeomorphism $\mathbb{RP}^1\cong S^1$ (via $\theta\mapsto 2\theta$). Therefore
$$\pi_1(\mathbb{RP}^1)\cong\pi_1(S^1)\cong\mathbb{Z}.$$

### Case $n\ge 2$: $\pi_1(\mathbb{RP}^n)\cong\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$

For $n\ge 2$, $S^n$ is simply connected: $\pi_1(S^n)=\{1\}$. We use the standard theorem relating the fundamental group of the base of a covering to the group of deck transformations / the fiber.

**Theorem (covering-space theory).** Let $p:\widetilde X\to X$ be a covering map with $\widetilde X$ path-connected and simply connected. Pick $\tilde x_0\in\widetilde X$, $x_0=p(\tilde x_0)$. Then the map
$$\Phi:\pi_1(X,x_0)\longrightarrow p^{-1}(x_0),\qquad [\gamma]\longmapsto \widetilde\gamma(1),$$
where $\widetilde\gamma$ is the unique lift of $\gamma$ starting at $\tilde x_0$, is a bijection of sets. Moreover, the group structure on $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ transports via $\Phi$ to a group structure on the fiber $p^{-1}(x_0)$, under which $\Phi$ is a group isomorphism (the fiber being identified with the group of deck transformations, which is isomorphic to $\pi_1(X)$ when $\widetilde X$ is the universal cover).

Applying this to $p:S^n\to\mathbb{RP}^n$ with $n\ge 2$:

- $\widetilde X=S^n$ is path-connected and simply connected (universal cover).
- The fiber over any point is $p^{-1}([x])=\{x,-x\}$, a 2-element set.

Therefore $\pi_1(\mathbb{RP}^n)$ is a group of order 2. The unique group of order 2 is $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$, so
$$\boxed{\pi_1(\mathbb{RP}^n)\cong\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}\quad(n\ge 2).}$$

**Identifying the nontrivial element explicitly.** The nontrivial loop is the image under $p$ of any path in $S^n$ from $x_0$ to $-x_0$ (a "half great circle"). Its square lifts to a loop in $S^n$ (going from $x_0$ to $-x_0$ and back to $x_0$), which is null-homotopic since $S^n$ is simply connected for $n\ge 2$. Hence the nontrivial element has order exactly 2, confirming $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$.

### Summary for $\mathbb{RP}^n$
$$\pi_1(\mathbb{RP}^n)\cong\begin{cases}\{1\}, & n=0,\\ \mathbb{Z}, & n=1,\\ \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}, & n\ge 2.\end{cases}$$

---

## Part II. $\pi_1(\mathrm{Kl}^2)$ (Klein bottle)

### Construction as a quotient of a square

The Klein bottle is obtained from the unit square $I^2=[0,1]^2$ by the identifications
$$(s,0)\sim(s,1)\quad\text{(top and bottom identified in the same direction, giving the "$b$" loop)},$$
$$(0,t)\sim(1,1-t)\quad\text{(left and right identified with a flip, giving the "$a$" loop)}.$$

Equivalently, reading the boundary word of the square starting from the lower-left corner going counterclockwise, the edge labels are
$$a\,b\,a^{-1}\,b,$$
so the single relator is $a\,b\,a^{-1}\,b=1$, i.e.
$$aba^{-1}b=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad aba^{-1}=b^{-1}.$$

### Applying the Seifert–van Kampen theorem

We use the standard CW-structure on the Klein bottle: one 0-cell $v$, two 1-cells $a$ and $b$ (the images of the horizontal and vertical edges), and one 2-cell attached along the word $aba^{-1}b$.

Let $X=\mathrm{Kl}^2$. Take a small open neighborhood $U$ of the 1-skeleton $X^{(1)}$ (a wedge of two circles, so $U$ deformation-retracts onto $S^1\vee S^1$) and let $V$ be the interior of the 2-cell (an open disk, contractible). Then $U\cap V$ is an open annulus, homotopy equivalent to $S^1$.

- $\pi_1(U)\cong\pi_1(S^1\vee S^1)\cong\langle a,b\rangle$ (free group on two generators).
- $\pi_1(V)=\{1\}$.
- $\pi_1(U\cap V)\cong\mathbb{Z}$, generated by a loop $\delta$ going once around the boundary of the 2-cell.

The inclusion $U\cap V\hookrightarrow U$ sends the generator $\delta$ to the boundary word $aba^{-1}b\in\langle a,b\rangle$. The inclusion $U\cap V\hookrightarrow V$ sends $\delta$ to $1$.

By the Seifert–van Kampen theorem,
$$\pi_1(\mathrm{Kl}^2)\cong\langle a,b\rangle\big/\langle\!\langle aba^{-1}b\rangle\!\rangle\cong\langle a,b\mid aba^{-1}b=1\rangle.$$

### The presentation

$$\boxed{\pi_1(\mathrm{Kl}^2)\cong\langle a,b\mid aba^{-1}b=1\rangle=\langle a,b\mid aba^{-1}=b^{-1}\rangle.}$$

### Structural remarks (non-abelian, distinguishing it from the torus)

The relation $aba^{-1}=b^{-1}$ shows that conjugation by $a$ inverts $b$. In particular $a$ and $b$ do **not** commute (otherwise $b=b^{-1}$, forcing $b^2=1$, which does not hold in this group). Hence $\pi_1(\mathrm{Kl}^2)$ is **non-abelian**, in contrast to $\pi_1(\mathbb{T}^2)\cong\mathbb{Z}^2$ (where the relation would be $aba^{-1}b^{-1}=1$).

**Abelianization.** Abelianizing imposes $ab=ba$, which together with $aba^{-1}b=1$ gives $b^2=1$ in the abelianization. So
$$\pi_1(\mathrm{Kl}^2)^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong\langle a,b\mid ab=ba,\; b^2=1\rangle\cong\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z},$$
with $a$ generating the $\mathbb{Z}$ factor and $b$ the $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ factor. This is consistent with $H_1(\mathrm{Kl}^2;\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$.

**Semidirect-product form.** The relation $aba^{-1}=b^{-1}$ expresses the group as a semidirect product
$$\pi_1(\mathrm{Kl}^2)\cong\langle b\rangle\rtimes\langle a\rangle\cong\mathbb{Z}\rtimes_{-1}\mathbb{Z},$$
where $a$ acts on $\langle b\rangle\cong\mathbb{Z}$ by inversion (the automorphism $n\mapsto -n$ of $\mathbb{Z}$). This is a clean, useful normal form: every element has a unique expression $b^m a^n$ with $m,n\in\mathbb{Z}$, and multiplication is governed by $a^n b^m = b^{(-1)^n m} a^n$.

### Verification that the presentation is infinite and non-abelian

The semidirect product $\mathbb{Z}\rtimes_{-1}\mathbb{Z}$ is a concrete infinite group satisfying exactly the relation $aba^{-1}b=1$ (with $b=(1,0)$, $a=(0,1)$, and the multiplication $(m,n)(m',n')=(m+(-1)^n m',\,n+n')$). It is infinite (the subgroup $\langle b\rangle\cong\mathbb{Z}$ is infinite) and non-abelian (since $ab=b^{-1}a\neq ba$). Being the universal group on two generators subject to the single relator $aba^{-1}b$, it is exactly $\pi_1(\mathrm{Kl}^2)$, confirming the presentation is correct and non-degenerate.

---

## Final answers

$$\pi_1(\mathbb{RP}^n)\cong\begin{cases}\{1\}, & n=0,\\ \mathbb{Z}, & n=1,\\ \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}, & n\ge 2,\end{cases}$$

and

$$\pi_1(\mathrm{Kl}^2)\cong\langle a,b\mid aba^{-1}b=1\rangle\cong\mathbb{Z}\rtimes_{-1}\mathbb{Z}.$$
